title: Before Pilate (John 18:28–19:16)
hook: Pilate asks what is truth and washes his hands

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's three denials, the rooster, and the Lord turning to look. Your line was the look was not anger. This morning, a governor.

Early morning. Jesus is led to the headquarters of the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. In John, the council tells Pilate they have no power to put anyone to death. That power is Rome's. What follows is almost a stage play. Pilate walks outside to the crowd, back inside to his prisoner, out again, in again. Outside, voices getting louder. Inside, a quiet man in chains, and a governor who can't work out who he is. And here's a strange thing: at Sunday Mass, in the Creed, Catholics say this man's name, a few words after the name of Mary. The old Apostles' Creed puts it: suffered under Pontius Pilate.
screen: `THE ROMAN GOVERNOR'S HOUSE.` → `OUT TO THE CROWD, BACK TO THE PRISONER.` → `SUFFERED UNDER PONTIUS PILATE.`

segments.voice: Pilate starts with the question that matters to Rome: are you a king? A king is a rival. Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world." Pilate presses. Jesus says he was born and came into the world to give testimony to the truth, and that everyone who is of the truth hears his voice. Then Pilate says the line: "What is truth?" And he doesn't wait. John says he goes straight back out. A sneer? Tired? An honest question? The text doesn't tell us his tone. Later readers found a wordplay in it: in Latin the question is quid est veritas, and shuffle those letters and you get est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here. Nobody in the story says that. But it's the Christian answer: the truth was standing in front of him. Three times Pilate says he finds no fault in him. And still he hands him over to be crucified. Matthew adds a picture: Pilate takes water and washes his hands in front of the crowd, as if that settled it. It didn't. The hands were washed; the choice was still his. It was Rome that carried out the execution. And the Catholic Church teaches plainly, at the Second Vatican Council and in its Catechism, that his death cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, or against the Jews of today.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.` · `WHAT IS TRUTH? HE DOESN'T WAIT.` · `NO FAULT IN HIM, AND HANDED OVER.` · `WATER DOESN'T WASH A CHOICE.` · then, large: `WHAT IS TRUTH?`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few weeks to a moment you knew something wasn't right and said, not my problem: a group chat that turned cruel, a coworker being talked about, a thing you could have said and didn't. No need to punish yourself; just see it clearly, the way you'd see water running over your hands. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to answer the question Pilate walked away from.
Before Pilate. The Roman governor who asked what truth is, found no fault, and washed his hands anyway. Today's word.
Your line: what is truth. That's Holy Week: palms, the tables, the perfume, the basin, the garden, the denials, and Pilate. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of the trial before Pilate every Good Friday, and they name Pilate each Sunday when they profess the Creed at Mass.

original.note: Greek: truth. the word in Pilate's question, and in Jesus's answer just before it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pilate washed his hands, so it wasn't his fault.
what it means: a man in power finds no fault, walks away from the question of truth, and hands him over anyway.
what a scholar hears: quid est veritas, and the later anagram est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here. and Rome, not a people, carried out the execution.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 18:36 and 18:38 given from memory; confirm.
The anagram 'est vir qui adest' is a later (medieval or later) wordplay, presented as such.
'Three times he finds no fault' (John 18:38, 19:4, 19:6). Confirm.
The handwashing is only in Matthew 27:24; the script says so. Paraphrased, not quoted.
Framing: Rome executed Jesus; CCC 597 and Nostra Aetate 4 on not blaming the Jewish people. Confirm wording is careful enough.

The Apostles' Creed line cited from the Book of Common Prayer 1662 as a public-domain English form; the Mass normally uses the Nicene Creed ('crucified under Pontius Pilate'), with the Apostles' Creed permitted. Keeper may prefer 'in the Creed' without a quotation.
